title: Preach the Word: I Have Kept the Faith
summary: Paul solemnly charges Timothy before God and Christ Jesus, the coming judge, to preach the word in every season, because a time is coming when people will turn from sound teaching to myths. Facing his own death, Paul says he is being poured out like a drink offering and that he has fought the good fight, finished the race, and kept the faith, and he looks to the crown of righteousness. He closes with personal news, requests for his cloak and scrolls, a warning about Alexander the coppersmith, and his testimony that when everyone deserted him at his first defense, the Lord stood by him.
story: This is the last chapter of Paul's last letter, and it reads like a final testament. It gathers the letter's themes into one charge (preach the word), sets Paul's approaching death beside his confidence in the coming day of Christ, and ends with a crowd of names: friends who have left, friends still at work, one who did great harm, and a few who send greetings. Acts ends with Paul in Rome proclaiming the kingdom; this chapter shows him there at the end, alone except for Luke, still concerned that the message be fully proclaimed. The torch passes to Timothy. Readers who follow the story of the early church have here the closest thing to Paul's final words.
historical:
Paul has already had a first defense (verse 16), probably a preliminary hearing before a Roman court, at which no one stood with him. He expects the outcome of his case to be death (verse 6). Early Christian tradition holds that Paul was executed in Rome under Nero, and because he was a Roman citizen, tradition says he was beheaded rather than crucified. Nero died in AD 68, so if Paul wrote this letter, it comes from the mid-60s. The phrase “delivered from the mouth of the lion” (verse 17) echoes Psalm 22:21 and is best taken as a picture of rescue from mortal danger, whether from immediate condemnation or from the power of the emperor, rather than literal lions; Roman citizens were not ordinarily thrown to beasts.

The people named are known from Paul's letters and Acts. Demas had been with Paul during an earlier imprisonment (Colossians 4:14; Philemon 24). Mark had left Paul and Barnabas on the first missionary trip, causing a sharp split (Acts 15:37-39), but was later reconciled and with Paul again (Colossians 4:10); now Paul calls him useful. Tychicus carried Paul's letters to Ephesus and Colossae (Ephesians 6:21; Colossians 4:7). Prisca (Priscilla) and Aquila were longtime coworkers (Acts 18; Romans 16:3). Erastus and Trophimus traveled with Paul (Acts 19:22; 20:4; 21:29). Of Eubulus, Pudens, Claudia, and Carpus nothing more is known with certainty. Irenaeus, in the late second century, names a Linus as the first leader of the Roman church after the apostles; this may be the same man, but it cannot be proved.
cultural:
Winter (verse 21) mattered because sea travel in the Mediterranean largely stopped from about November to March, when storms made voyages dangerous (compare Acts 27:9-12). If Timothy did not come soon, he might not reach Rome until spring. A Roman prison could be cold and dark, which is why Paul wants his cloak, a heavy outer garment. The scrolls and parchments (verse 13) were the books of the ancient world. Parchment was prepared animal skin, more durable and more expensive than papyrus, and was used for valued texts and for notebooks. What Paul's parchments contained is unknown; suggestions include copies of the Jewish Scriptures, his own notes, or legal documents.

The drink offering (verse 6) was part of Israel's sacrificial worship: wine was poured out at the altar alongside other offerings (Numbers 15:1-10), and pagan worshipers also poured libations to their gods. Paul had used the same image in Philippians 2:17. The word for departure (analusis) was used of loosing a ship from its moorings or striking a tent, a gentle picture for death. The crown (stephanos) was the wreath given to a victorious athlete, and the race and the fight (verse 7) were images from the games.
literary: The chapter has three parts. Verses 1-5 are the solemn charge, introduced by an oath-like formula before God and Christ Jesus, who will judge the living and the dead. Five sharp commands (preach, be prepared, reprove, rebuke, encourage) are followed by a reason (people will turn to myths) and four more commands. Verses 6-8 are Paul's farewell, built on three parallel clauses in verse 7 and looking forward to the crown in verse 8. Verses 9-22 are personal notes and greetings. The chapter alternates between the solemn and the ordinary: a charge before the judge of the world, and a request for a coat. Both belong to the same life. Verses 16-18 form a small testimony of their own, moving from desertion by everyone, to the Lord's standing by, to confidence in his heavenly kingdom and a doxology.

outline.t: The solemn charge: preach the word
Poured out: the good fight, the finished race, the crown
Come quickly: who has left, who remains, and what to bring
Deserted by all, but the Lord stood by me

doctrines.note: Christ Jesus “will judge the living and the dead” (verse 1), and the Lord is “the righteous Judge” (verse 8). The coming judgment gives weight to Timothy's ministry and hope to Paul's death.

The crown of righteousness is laid up not only for Paul but “to all who crave His appearing” (verse 8). The Christian's hope is not merely surviving death but being brought safely into the Lord's heavenly kingdom (verse 18).

Timothy is to preach the word in season and out of season and to carry out the evangelist's task. Even at his first defense, Paul saw the Lord's purpose that the message be fully proclaimed and that all the Gentiles hear it (verse 17).

words.note: Spendō, to pour out as a drink offering. Paul pictures his coming death as a sacrifice poured out to God, the last act of a life offered in worship. The present tense (“I am already being poured out”) shows that he sees the process as already underway.

Analusis, departure, found only here in the New Testament. It was used for untying a boat or breaking camp. For Paul, death is not an end but a setting out, which matches his words in Philippians 1:23 about his desire to depart and be with Christ.

Stephanos, a crown or victor's wreath, distinct from a royal diadem. It was awarded to athletes who won their races. The crown of righteousness may mean the crown that consists in righteousness or the crown given by the righteous Judge; in either case it is the reward of faithful endurance, given by grace.

Euangelistēs, evangelist, one who proclaims the good news. The word appears only three times in the New Testament (here, Acts 21:8 of Philip, and Ephesians 4:11). Timothy is to do this work as part of his ministry, not leaving it to others.

christ: The chapter holds Christ Jesus before Timothy as judge and king: he “will judge the living and the dead,” and his appearing and his kingdom frame the charge (verse 1). The crown is given by “the Lord, the righteous Judge” to all who long for his appearing (verse 8). Paul's final testimony is about Christ's faithfulness when everyone else failed: “the Lord stood by me and strengthened me” (verse 17). His own experience echoes that of Jesus, who was deserted by his friends before his trial and yet was not alone because the Father was with him (John 16:32). Like Jesus on the cross, Paul asks that those who failed him not be held accountable (verse 16; compare Luke 23:34). And his confidence that the Lord will bring him safely into his heavenly kingdom (verse 18) rests on the one who has already abolished death (1:10).

hard.q: How can Paul say “The Lord will repay him according to his deeds” about Alexander, and then pray that others not be held accountable?
hard.a:
Verse 14 about Alexander and verse 16 about those who deserted Paul sit close together and can seem inconsistent. The difference lies in what each did. Those who failed to stand with Paul at his hearing acted out of fear, and he forgives them as one who knows human weakness. Alexander, by contrast, did Paul great harm and vigorously opposed the message itself (verse 15). Paul's words about him echo Psalm 62:12 and Proverbs 24:12, which say that God repays each according to what he has done. Paul does not take revenge; he leaves judgment to the Lord, as he taught in Romans 12:19, and he warns Timothy to protect himself.

Some readers still feel a tension between this and Jesus' command to pray for enemies. Many interpreters answer that entrusting an unrepentant enemy of the gospel to God's just judgment is not the same as wishing him harm; it is the stance of the psalms and of the souls under the altar in Revelation 6:10, who leave vengeance to God. Paul's own example holds both together: mercy for the weak, and trust in God's justice concerning those who fight against the truth.

questions: Paul charges Timothy to preach the word “in season and out of season.” What makes it hard to be faithful when the message is unwelcome?
Paul could say he had fought the good fight, finished the race, and kept the faith. What would you need to change now in order to say the same at the end of your life?
Paul's last letter ends with a list of names and a request for a coat and books. What does that tell you about how ordinary needs and friendships fit into a life given to God?
